import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 307

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
-/

namespace Erdos307

open scoped Finset

/--
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_307 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime : answer(True) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧
    Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  show True ↔ _
  simp only [Finset.mem_inter, not_and, true_iff]
  use {1, 5}, {2, 3}
  norm_num +decide

/--
There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
    1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`,
the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and
nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no
`native_decide` enters this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean#L121"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) (hQne : Q.Nonempty)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    59 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) ∧ (4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2 := by
  sorry

end Erdos307

findings.description: The docstring at line 79 says “so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`,” presenting this as a consequence of the machine-checked bound. The declaration actually states `(4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2`, which corresponds to the rounded lower bound `2·10⁵⁶`, not `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The theorem and its formal_proof attribution are correct; only the docstring conflates the rounded formal result with the sharper paper result.
findings.source_evidence: The cited Closed.lean, at commit 76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b, explicitly says: “The paper's `thm:barrier` states the sharp `2.09·10⁵⁶`; what is machine-checked here is the rounded `2·10⁵⁶` ... The sharp value is a paper result, not a Lean one.” See https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean, lines 11–14. The paper's barrier theorem separately gives the sharper bound.
findings.suggested_fix: Change `2.09·10⁵⁶` in the final inference to `2·10⁵⁶`. Alternatively, state separately that the paper establishes the sharper bound, without attributing that constant to this machine-checked theorem. Leave the Lean statement and formal_proof attribute unchanged.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses natural-number sets, excludes zero only from the intersection, and requires at least two elements in each set. The source asks the positive-integer coprime question and supplies nontrivial examples, without explicit cardinality conditions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under the Lean conditions, zero cannot belong to either set. If 0 belongs to P, pairwise coprimality and #P > 1 force P = {0,1}, whose reciprocal sum is 1. The intersection condition makes Q positive, so the product equation forces its reciprocal sum to be 1. An integral reciprocal sum with pairwise-coprime positive denominators forces every denominator to equal 1, contradicting #Q > 1. The symmetric argument excludes zero from Q. Thus the intersection restriction is pointwise equivalent to excluding zero from the union when the remaining conditions hold. The extra cardinality conditions do not change the existential answer: the source's explicit witness P = {1,5}, Q = {2,3} satisfies them. Both the pointwise zero-condition equivalence and the existential equivalence with the positive-integer source formulation were proved in scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Instead of explicitly requiring denominators to be integers at least 2, Lean combines `0 ∉ P ∩ Q`, `1 ∉ P ∪ Q`, pairwise coprimality, and cardinalities greater than 1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The formulations are pointwise equivalent. A pairwise-coprime set containing 0 can have no other element except 1; excluding 1 and requiring two elements therefore excludes 0 individually. Conversely, for positive denominators unequal to 1, the equation excludes empty sets. A singleton P = {a} would force the other reciprocal sum to equal the integer a. This is impossible for a nonempty pairwise-coprime set of denominators at least 2: isolating any reciprocal shows its denominator divides the product of the other denominators, contradicting coprimality. Thus the source's conditions already imply both cardinality restrictions. The full pointwise equivalence was proved as Review307.no_one_iff_source.

reformulations.difference: The rounded barrier is expressed as a squared bound for P, with an explicit Q.Nonempty hypothesis, rather than ordinary lower bounds for both prime products.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The equation itself forces both sets to be nonempty. Their products are nonnegative, and `(2·10^56)^2 = 4·10^112`, so the squared bound is equivalent to the ordinary rounded bound. Applying the universally quantified theorem with P and Q exchanged gives the same bound for Q. I proved the equivalence of the universal squared formulation and the rounded two-sided minimum formulation as Review307.barrier_forms_equivalent. This equivalence concerns 2·10^56, not the sharper constant mentioned in the docstring.

review.notes: All four explicit declarations were checked. The source still records the prime problem and the coprime variant excluding 1 as open; the positive coprime answer matches its examples. In /workspace/review/external_all.lean, I recompiled the cited barrier proof and its dependency chain and derived the exact repository statement. Its axiom report contains only propext, Classical.choice, and Quot.sound. Scratch tests verified both source examples, empty/zero/singleton cases, and absence of prime-set solutions using primes at most 13. No statement-level misformalization was found. The original 1976 Barbeau journal item was not retrieved; its posed problem was checked against the cited Erdős page and its LaTeX statement.
